definitions.def: Having lost your job because the role is no longer needed
definitions.description: Used in British English when a company removes a position – not because the person performed badly, but because the job itself no longer exists. Always used as 'made redundant'.
examples: He was made redundant last spring when the company moved its operations abroad.
The company plans to make the whole department redundant next quarter.

definitions.def: No longer needed or useful
definitions.description: Something is redundant when it repeats or duplicates what already exists, making it unnecessary.
examples: The second paragraph is redundant – it just repeats the introduction.
With GPS on every phone, printed maps have become largely redundant.

definitions.def: To annoy or bother someone, often repeatedly
definitions.description: Used when something causes mild but persistent annoyance. The noun is irritation, the adjective is irritating (the cause) or irritated (the feeling you have).
examples: It really irritates me when people are late without letting you know.
His constant interruptions irritated her more than she wanted to admit.
The noise from the construction site was starting to irritate the whole office.

definitions.def: To cause discomfort or soreness to a part of the body
definitions.description: Used when something causes a physical reaction – skin, eyes, throat etc.
examples: Cheap washing powder can irritate sensitive skin.
The smoke from the bonfire was beginning to irritate his eyes.

definitions.def: A feeling of strong hostility or deep hatred between people or groups
definitions.description: More than just disliking someone – a lasting, serious mutual hostility. Unlike hatred, enmity usually implies both sides feel it. More common in writing than casual speech.
examples: There was a long-standing enmity between the two families that nobody could fully explain.
Despite their professional enmity, they managed to work together on the project.
The enmity between the two rival gangs had lasted for decades.

definitions.def: Physically weak and delicate, often due to old age or illness
definitions.description: Used to describe someone whose body is weak and fragile – not strong enough to cope with much physical strain. Adds the idea of being easily hurt, like something delicate.
examples: His grandmother had become increasingly frail in her final years.
She looked frail after months in hospital, but her mind was as sharp as ever.
The old man was too frail to climb the stairs without help.

definitions.def: Dead or decaying flesh of an animal, especially when eaten by scavengers
definitions.description: Mostly used in nature and wildlife contexts. Vultures, crows, and hyenas are classic carrion eaters. Can also be used figuratively to describe something rotten or corrupt.
examples: Vultures circled high above, searching for carrion on the plain.
The smell of carrion drew scavengers from miles around.
Carrion beetles play an important role in breaking down dead animals in the wild.

definitions.def: An animal or person that feeds on dead animals, waste, or leftovers rather than hunting fresh prey
definitions.description: Most commonly used in wildlife contexts – vultures, hyenas, and crows are classic scavengers. Can also describe a person who searches through rubbish or abandoned places for useful things.
examples: Hyenas are often scavengers, feeding on the kills of other predators.
After the storm, scavengers picked through the wreckage looking for anything valuable.
The crow is one of nature's most adaptable scavengers.

definitions.def: Lacking physical strength or energy
definitions.description: Similar to frail but emphasises lack of power rather than fragility. The person simply cannot do much.
examples: The old man's voice was so feeble we could barely hear him.
She made a feeble attempt to lift the box but had to ask for help.
After weeks in bed, his legs felt feeble and unsteady.

definitions.def: Weak and unconvincing – failing to impress
definitions.description: Used about arguments, excuses or efforts that simply don't cut it. Very common in everyday British English.
examples: That's a pretty feeble excuse – you could have called to let us know.
His attempt at humour was so feeble that nobody laughed.
The government's response to the crisis was widely criticised as feeble.

definitions.def: One of the coloured leaf-like parts of a flower
definitions.description: The soft, coloured parts that make up the head of a flower. Roses, tulips, sunflowers all have petals.
examples: She pulled the petals off a daisy one by one.
The rose petals scattered across the floor as the bouquet dried out.
After the storm, the garden was covered in fallen petals.

definitions.def: A warm term of affection used to address someone fondly
definitions.description: Used as a warm, affectionate nickname – similar to love, darling, or sweetheart. Very common in the North of England especially.
examples: Don't worry, petal – everything will be fine.
What's the matter, petal? You look upset.
Come here, petal, let me have a look at that.

definitions.def: Free to do something – permitted or allowed
definitions.description: Used when someone has permission or freedom to act. Most commonly heard in the negative – 'I'm not at liberty to...' – meaning you are not allowed to share or do something. Very common in formal and professional British English.
examples: I'm not at liberty to discuss the details of the case.
You are at liberty to leave whenever you wish.
She felt she was not at liberty to share what she knew.

definitions.def: Friendly and peaceful, without hostility – especially in situations that could be tense
definitions.description: Used when two people or groups deal with each other cooperatively despite potential conflict. Common in legal, business and relationship contexts. Used about situations, not people directly – say 'amicable divorce' not 'amicable person'.
examples: The two companies reached an amicable agreement without going to court.
Despite the divorce, they managed to remain amicable for the sake of their children.
The dispute was settled in an amicable manner, with both sides satisfied.

definitions.def: Having a friendly, pleasant and good-natured character
definitions.description: Used to describe people who are easy to get along with, warm and likeable. Key difference from amicable: amiable describes people and personality, amicable describes situations and agreements.
examples: He was an amiable fellow – always smiling and ready for a chat.
The new manager had an amiable manner that put everyone at ease.
She came across as amiable and approachable, which made her popular with clients.
The amiable shopkeeper greeted every customer by name.
Despite the long delay, the amiable host kept everyone entertained.

definitions.def: Extremely small in size
definitions.description: Used to describe something or someone noticeably small – often with a sense of charm or delicateness. More formal and literary than simply saying 'small' or 'tiny'.
examples: Despite her diminutive frame, she was one of the strongest athletes on the team.
The old town was full of diminutive cottages with low doorways and tiny windows.
He was a diminutive figure standing in the corner of the vast conference hall.
A diminutive kitten appeared at the doorstep, soaking wet from the rain.
The diminutive jockey guided the horse with remarkable confidence and skill.

definitions.def: A shorter, affectionate form of a name or word
definitions.description: A word or name formed to express smallness or affection – such as 'Charlie' from 'Charles' or 'kitchenette' from 'kitchen'.
examples: 'Liz' is a common diminutive of 'Elizabeth'.
'Will' and 'Bill' are both diminutives of 'William'.
Teachers often use diminutives when addressing younger children – 'Alex' instead of 'Alexander'.
'Booklet' is a diminutive of 'book' – the suffix '-let' making it smaller.
In informal speech, diminutives make names feel warmer and more personal.

definitions.def: Slightly wet – not soaking but noticeably moist
definitions.description: Something that has absorbed some moisture but isn't fully wet. Very common in British English given the climate. Damp is more unpleasant than 'moist' – moist is neutral or pleasant, damp implies discomfort.
examples: The clothes were still damp after an hour in the dryer.
She wiped the table with a damp cloth.
The walls felt damp – a sign the building had poor insulation.
His hair was still damp from the shower when he left the house.
The cellar smelled damp and musty, as if it hadn't been opened in years.

definitions.def: Cold and moist – used about weather or atmosphere
definitions.description: Describes that typical grey, cold, moist feeling in the air. Very much a British weather word.
examples: It was one of those grey, damp November mornings that makes you want to stay in bed.
The damp air off the Thames made the evening feel much colder than it was.
London in February is almost always cold and damp.
They walked through the damp streets, their breath visible in the cold air.
The damp weather had settled in for the week with no sign of sun.

definitions.def: To make something slightly wet
definitions.description: The verb form of damp. You dampen something when you add a little moisture, but not enough to soak it. Common with cloths, sponges, hair and soil.
examples: Dampen the cloth slightly before you wipe the screen.
She dampened her hair with a spray bottle before styling it.
He dampened the sponge and ran it along the shelf.
Dampen the soil gently so the seeds do not wash away.
A light mist of rain dampened the pavement but did not stop the match.

definitions.def: To reduce enthusiasm, excitement or a good mood
definitions.description: Very common in British English with words like mood, spirits, enthusiasm and excitement. It usually follows bad news, bad weather or criticism. Often used in the negative: nothing could dampen something.
examples: The bad news dampened the mood at the office.
Nothing could dampen her excitement about the trip.
The rain dampened everyone's spirits at the outdoor event.
His harsh criticism dampened her enthusiasm for the project.
Even the setbacks could not dampen their determination to finish.

definitions.def: To make a sound or vibration weaker
definitions.description: Used in engineering, music and acoustics. Foam, rubber or thick fabric dampens noise and vibration. The related noun is damping.
examples: Thick carpets help to dampen the noise from the flat upstairs.
The drummer dampened the cymbal with his hand.
Rubber feet dampen the vibration from the washing machine.
The studio walls are lined with foam to dampen echoes.
A heavy curtain will dampen the sound of traffic at night.

definitions.def: Located at or towards the back of something
definitions.description: Used in medical and scientific contexts to mean 'at the back' – the opposite of anterior (front). Part of a Latin word family: anterior (front), posterior (back), superior (above), inferior (below).
examples: The posterior part of the brain controls vision and spatial awareness.
The injury was located in the posterior region of the shoulder.
The surgeon made an incision along the posterior wall of the cavity.
Posterior ligament damage is often harder to detect than anterior injuries.
The posterior lobe of the pituitary gland regulates several key hormones.

definitions.def: A polite or humorous word for the buttocks
definitions.description: Formal Latin-origin word used either medically or with a light humorous tone – a polite way to say 'bottom'.
examples: He slipped on the ice and landed squarely on his posterior.
She gave him a gentle kick on the posterior to get him moving.
The toddler waddled across the room, his posterior swaying with each step.
The doctor asked him to lie on his side so she could examine the posterior.
He patted the dog on its posterior and sent it running back to its owner.

definitions.def: A sample or example of something taken for examination or study
definitions.description: Most commonly used in scientific, medical or biological contexts. A single example taken to represent or analyse the whole. In forensic contexts, specimens are collected from crime scenes for laboratory analysis.
examples: The doctor asked him to provide a urine specimen before the appointment.
Scientists collected rock specimens from the cave floor for analysis.
The museum displayed a rare specimen of a prehistoric fish perfectly preserved in amber.
The nurse labelled each specimen carefully before sending it to the laboratory.
The investigation faltered when experts couldn't find any evidence in the specimens from the crime scene.

definitions.def: Closely packed together – with little space between parts
definitions.description: Used when things are tightly packed – crowds, forests, fog, materials. The opposite of sparse or thin.
examples: The explorers struggled to move through the dense jungle, hacking through thick vegetation.
A dense crowd had gathered outside the theatre long before the doors opened.
The city centre was covered in a dense fog that made driving almost impossible.
Dense woodland surrounded the village on all sides, cutting it off from the outside world.
The material was incredibly dense – a small block of it weighed several kilograms.

definitions.def: Slow to understand – not very intelligent
definitions.description: Used informally to call someone a bit dim or slow-witted. Said with mild frustration, often affectionately. Similar to thick or dim in British English.
examples: He read the instructions three times and still couldn't follow them – he was being incredibly dense.
'Don't be dense!' she laughed, explaining the joke for the second time.
I felt a bit dense asking such an obvious question in front of everyone.
He's not dense – he just needs things explained slowly and clearly.
She gave him a look that said she thought he was being wilfully dense.

definitions.def: Difficult to understand – complex and heavy
definitions.description: Used about text, lectures or ideas that are packed with complexity and hard to get through.
examples: The professor's lecture was so dense that most students struggled to keep up.
It's a dense read – every paragraph contains three ideas worth thinking about.
The legal document was dense with technical language that only a specialist could follow.
His writing style is famously dense – rewarding but demanding.
The report was dense with statistics and required careful reading.

definitions.def: To destroy something completely – leaving nothing behind
definitions.description: The strongest word for total destruction. When something is obliterated it is wiped out entirely, as if it never existed. Used about physical destruction – cities, buildings, armies.
examples: The medieval town was obliterated by bombing raids, leaving nothing but rubble.
The earthquake obliterated entire villages in the region.
The fire spread so quickly that it obliterated the warehouse within minutes.
The invading army obliterated every settlement in its path as it advanced.
A single asteroid impact obliterated the dinosaurs along with three quarters of all life on Earth.

definitions.def: To remove or wipe out completely – memories, records, traces
definitions.description: Used when something disappears so completely that no trace remains – memories, evidence, inscriptions. Powerful and permanent.
examples: Years of therapy couldn't obliterate the memories of what he had witnessed.
The new development obliterated any trace of the Victorian street that had once stood there.
She obliterated all evidence of the relationship – deleting photos and messages.
His name was obliterated from the records as if he had never worked there.
Time had obliterated the inscription on the ancient gravestone.

definitions.def: To defeat someone overwhelmingly
definitions.description: Used informally about sport or competition – winning so decisively that the opponent is completely crushed.
examples: The home team obliterated their opponents, winning 7–0 in a stunning performance.
She obliterated the competition at the chess tournament, winning every single match.
The new product obliterated its rivals in sales figures within the first month.
He obliterated the world record by nearly four seconds – an astonishing achievement.
The debate performance obliterated his opponent's credibility entirely.

definitions.def: A tool or implement used for a practical task – especially in cooking or eating
definitions.description: Most commonly used about kitchen tools and eating implements. In British English, knives/forks/spoons are often called cutlery specifically, while utensils refers more broadly to any handheld cooking or eating tool.
examples: She laid out the utensils neatly beside each plate – knife, fork and spoon.
The kitchen drawer was crammed with utensils he'd bought but never used.
A wooden spoon is one of the most versatile cooking utensils you can own.
He couldn't find a single clean utensil – every pan and spoon was piled in the sink.
The camping kit included basic utensils – a tin cup, a fork and a small folding knife.

definitions.def: A feeling of self-consciousness or shyness that stops you behaving naturally
definitions.description: An inner barrier that holds you back from doing or saying something freely. Often used in the plural – 'inhibitions'. The opposite is uninhibited – free and open with no barriers.
examples: After a couple of drinks he lost his inhibitions and got up to dance.
She was a naturally shy child with many inhibitions around strangers.
The drama class helped students shed their inhibitions and express themselves freely.
He had no inhibitions whatsoever – he'd say exactly what he thought to anyone.
Growing up in a strict household gave her deep inhibitions about showing emotion in public.

definitions.def: The restraining or slowing down of a process
definitions.description: Used in psychology, biology and medicine to describe the suppression of a function, impulse or process.
examples: The drug works through the inhibition of certain enzymes in the brain.
Stress causes inhibition of the immune system, making the body more vulnerable to illness.
The study examined the inhibition of nerve signals in patients with chronic pain.
Chemical inhibition of the bacteria prevented the infection from spreading further.
The inhibition of aggressive impulses is a key part of socialisation in early childhood.
